quirks: Statewide birth and death registration began in 1919 (general compliance by 1928 for births, 1922 for deaths); no civil birth or death records exist before those dates — use federal census, church records, and delayed birth certificates as substitutes for 1900-1919 events. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records

Records for African Americans were kept in separate files with separate indexes throughout this period. The Spalding County marriage volumes on FamilySearch include dedicated 'colored' registers: volume F (imageGroupNumber 007718973, 1903-1910, 100% name-indexed) and volume I (imageGroupNumber 007718976, 1923-1933/1932-1937, 100% name-indexed). A 1905 African American marriage must be sought in volume F, not the general register. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records
The Spalding County Courthouse burned in 1874 and 1981, but ALL records survived both fires — no record loss. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy

The 1920 and 1930 federal censuses for Spalding County are 0% name-indexed on FamilySearch (browse-only image groups 004300135 and 004532000); use Ancestry or other indexed databases for name searches in these years.

Neighboring counties (Butts, Clayton, Coweta, Fayette, Henry, Lamar, Meriwether, Pike) may hold records for extended family; search those county marriage and probate records if Spalding yields nothing. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy

Eloping couples sometimes married in an alternate county — if the 1905 Ogletree-Pearcy marriage is not in Spalding County, check neighboring Pike and Henry Counties. Per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records
Marriage records for Spalding County are well-preserved and well-indexed on FamilySearch; all volumes 1898-1942 are 100% name-indexed.
The Great Migration brought many Spalding County African American families to Chicago c.1916-1940; children born after migration appear in Illinois records, not Georgia ones.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Spalding County, Georgia (1900-1940)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 20, 1851 from Fayette, Henry, and Pike Counties
- **County seat:** Griffin, Georgia
- **Population:** 17,619 (1900) → 19,741 (1910) → 21,908 (1920) → 23,495 (1930) → 28,427 (1940)
- **Economy:** Cotton agriculture, textile mills, railroad junction
- **Ethnic composition:** Significant African American population; the Ogletree/Pearcy family is almost certainly African American based on the separate 'colored' marriage register and Great Migration pattern
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (predominant among African Americans), Methodist, Presbyterian

## Boundary changes
Boundaries stable throughout 1900-1940. No predecessor searches needed.
Neighboring counties: Butts, Clayton, Coweta, Fayette, Henry, Lamar, Meriwether, Pike.

## Vital records
- **Births (civil):** Statewide registration began 1919; general compliance by 1928. No county birth records before 1919.
- **Deaths (civil):** Statewide registration began 1919; general compliance by 1922.
- **Marriages:** County records begin 1852 (county organization).
- **African American marriage registers:** Separate 'colored' volumes. Volume F (1903-1910, 100% indexed) and Volume I (1923-1933, 100% indexed) on FamilySearch.

## Federal censuses
- 1900: 96-97% name-indexed on FamilySearch
- 1910: Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- 1920: 0% indexed on FamilySearch (browse-only); indexed on Ancestry
- 1930: 0% indexed on FamilySearch (browse-only); indexed on Ancestry
- 1940: Indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

## Record losses
None — all records survived courthouse fires in 1874 and 1981.

## Key collections on FamilySearch
- Georgia County Marriages 1785-1950 (indexed+images)
- Georgia Deaths 1914-1927 and 1928-1943 (indexed+images)
- Georgia County Delayed Birth and Death Records 1829-1961 (indexed+images)
- Georgia Probate Records 1742-1990 (indexed+images)
- WWII Draft Cards 1940-1945 (indexed+images)

## Research tips
1. No civil births before 1919 — use census, church records, delayed birth certificates
2. African American records in separate indexes — search 'colored' marriage volumes specifically
3. The 1905 Ogletree-Pearcy marriage is in volume F (imageGroupNumber 007718973)
4. Children born after migration to Chicago appear in Illinois, not Georgia records
5. Church records (especially Baptist) are primary pre-1919 substitute for vital records
6. Step-by-step guides: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Step-by-Step_Georgia_Research,_1880-Present

# Locality Guide: Cook County, Illinois (1900–1945)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1831 from unorganized territory
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Chicago was the second-largest U.S. city throughout this period; Cook County population grew from roughly 1.8 million (1900) to over 4 million (1940) driven by industry and immigration, including the Great Migration of African Americans from the South (c. 1916–1940)
- **Economy:** Meatpacking (Union Stock Yards), steel, manufacturing, railroads, commerce; major industrial employer base drew both European immigrants and African American migrants
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, German, Polish, Italian, Czech, African American (Great Migration), Scandinavian, and many other groups; by 1930 Chicago had one of the largest African American urban populations in the country
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (large Irish, Polish, Italian parishes), Baptist and AME (African American congregations), Lutheran (German, Scandinavian), Methodist, Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** 1871 Chicago Fire (destroyed nearly all pre-1871 records); 1893 World's Columbian Exposition; 1919 race riots; Great Migration 1916–1940; Great Depression 1929–1939; World War II 1941–1945

## Boundary changes
- Cook County was established in 1831 and its boundaries have remained substantially stable through the target period. No major boundary changes affected the county during 1900–1945.
- The county encompasses the City of Chicago (incorporated 1837) and numerous townships and suburban municipalities.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Cook County began recording births and deaths at the **county** level in 1877. Statewide mandatory registration began in 1916 for both births and deaths (compliance improved to near-complete by 1919 for deaths, 1922 for births). Marriages have been recorded at the county level since county formation (1831).
- **What exists:** Births 1871–present (county registers 1871–1915; county certificates 1871–1953); Deaths 1871–1998 (county level); Marriages 1871–1969 (county level); Illinois statewide Deaths and Stillbirths 1916–1948
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized, see collections below); Illinois State Archives (Springfield); Cook County Clerk's office (Chicago) for recent records
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 records destroyed in the 1871 Chicago Fire. Birth registration compliance was incomplete before c. 1922 — many births before that date were not registered at the time (delayed birth certificates filed later). African Americans may be in separate registers or indexes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal records (Catholic parishes have excellent sacramental registers); newspaper birth announcements in the Chicago Defender (African American press); midwife records
- **FamilySearch collections:**
  - Cook County Birth Registers 1871–1915 (collection id 1463129)
  - Cook County Birth Certificates 1871–1953 (collection id 1462519)
  - Cook County Deaths 1871–1998 (collection id 1463134)
  - Cook County Marriages 1871–1969 (collection id 1463145)
  - Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths 1916–1948 (collection id 1438856)
  - Illinois County Marriages 1810–1940 (collection id 1803970)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (large sacramental registers by parish, many in Polish, Italian, or German); Baptist (African American congregations such as Olivet Baptist, Pilgrim Baptist); African Methodist Episcopal; Methodist; Lutheran; Jewish synagogue records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Individual parishes; Catholic Archdiocese of Chicago Archives (has many consolidated registers); denominational archives; some microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Language:** English for most Protestant records; Latin and vernacular (Polish, Italian, German) for Catholic sacramental records

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1900 (85–96% name-indexed on FamilySearch for Cook County volumes); 1910 (indexed); 1920 (indexed); 1930 (indexed); 1940 (indexed with full-text search available). 1880 available and indexed. **1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed nationwide** — no Cook County 1890 census exists.
- **State census:** Illinois did not conduct state-level censuses during this period
- **Other enumerations:** Chicago city directories (published annually; available on Ancestry and microfilm) serve as annual substitutes for census years
- **Access:** Federal census years 1900–1940 are indexed and searchable by name on FamilySearch and Ancestry. African American households may be enumerated on separate enumeration district pages; search by ED if name search fails.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; Cook County Circuit Court records
- **Date range:** 1831–present (pre-1871 records destroyed in Chicago Fire)
- **Where held:** Cook County Circuit Court Clerk's office; Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University for older records; FamilySearch has Illinois Probate Records 1819–1988 (collection id 1834344)
- **Digitization:** FamilySearch collection 1834344 covers Cook County probate; indexing level varies by volume

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (Public Land Survey System — federal-land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original patents issued by the U.S. General Land Office; subsequent deeds recorded at the county level by the Cook County Recorder of Deeds
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, patents, tax records
- **Date range:** Federal land patents from the 1830s; county deed records from 1831 (pre-1871 records destroyed in Chicago Fire)
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (Chicago); Bureau of Land Management GLO Records (online, glorecords.blm.gov) for original patents; Illinois State Archives

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** World War I (1917–1918), World War II (1941–1945)
- **Record types:** WWI draft registration cards (1917–1918, on Ancestry/FamilySearch); WWII draft registration cards 1940–1945 (FamilySearch collection id 2832983); service records at NARA; Illinois adjutant general records
- **Where held:** NARA (St. Louis for service records; Washington DC for pension files); FamilySearch and Ancestry for draft cards; Illinois State Archives for state military records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery; Rosehill Cemetery; Oak Woods Cemetery (large African American section); Lincoln Cemetery (historically African American); Mount Carmel; many Catholic parish cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have Cook County coverage; Oak Woods and Lincoln Cemetery are particularly important for African American families
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries; Chicago Death Index (compiled from death certificates)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (1847–present); Chicago Daily News; Chicago Defender (1905–present — African American press, essential for Black Chicago families); Chicago Broad Ax; Chicago Whip
- **Where held:** Chicago Tribune and Defender archives online (ProQuest Historical Newspapers); Defender microfilm at Chicago Public Library and other libraries; Chronicling America (Library of Congress) for some early papers
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, death notices, community events; the Chicago Defender is particularly valuable for African American families and carries announcements, social notices, and migrant arrival notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland — most immigrants arrived via East Coast ports (New York/Ellis Island, Baltimore, Boston) or Canadian ports then traveled inland; some via Great Lakes ports (Milwaukee, Detroit)
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (at arrival port, not Chicago); naturalization records filed in Cook County Circuit Court; declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization; alien registration (1940)
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists digitized on Ancestry/FamilySearch); Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records; FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **Note for African American families:** African American migrants from the South were not immigrants in the legal sense; passenger lists do not apply. Their movement from Georgia to Chicago is documented in census records, city directories, and the Chicago Defender's 'Arrivals' column.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Cook County property tax records; personal property
- **Date range:** 1831–present (pre-1871 records destroyed)
- **Where held:** Cook County Assessor's office; Illinois State Archives; some records at IRAD
- **Substitute value:** Annual property tax records can help track residence between census years

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Chicago city directories published annually are essential finding aids; available on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and microfilm at Chicago Public Library. They list head of household, occupation, and address — the closest substitute for off-census years.
- **Scott's Blue Book:** African American business and social directory published 1939–1965; lists Black Chicago residents, businesses, churches, and organizations. Key resource for Ogletree/Pearcy family research.
- **Chicago Defender 'Migrants' column:** The Defender regularly listed new arrivals from the South by name and city of origin — search for Ogletree/Pearcy arrivals c. 1916–1930.
- **Social welfare and institutional records:** Cook County Hospital records; Chicago Urban League records (assisted African American migrants); YMCA records; settlement house records
- **School records:** Chicago Public Schools enrollment records; some available through Chicago Public Schools archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Cook County births, deaths, marriages (1871–1953/1969/1998); Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths 1916–1948; Illinois Probate 1819–1988; WWII Draft Cards; federal censuses 1880–1940 | Free |
| Ancestry | Cook County vital records; federal censuses; Chicago city directories; WWI/WWII draft cards; Illinois naturalization records | Subscription |
| ProQuest Historical Newspapers | Chicago Tribune; Chicago Defender (1905–1975) | Library subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Selected early Illinois newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO Records | Original federal land patents | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 18,593 total digitized volumes matching Cook County, Illinois; only the first page of results was examined. The 8 collections detailed above are confirmed from collections_search and represent major vital, military, and probate series. Many additional volumes — including city directories, church records, and specialized record sets — exist in the full result set but were not individually examined.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Cook County Clerk's Office, Chicago | Vital records (marriages, recent births/deaths) | In-person / online portal |
| Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County Circuit Court records, older county records | In-person / mail |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | Statewide vital records, state military records | In-person / online portal |
| Chicago Public Library — Harold Washington Library Center | City directories, newspapers, microfilm | In-person |
| Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection, Chicago Public Library (Woodson Branch) | African American genealogy and history collections; Chicago Defender clippings; community organization records | In-person; contact for mail research |
| Newberry Library, Chicago | Manuscript collections, city directories, historical records | In-person |
| Catholic Archdiocese of Chicago Archives | Parish sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | By appointment / mail request |
| NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago | Federal records, naturalization files, some military records | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1871 records (destroyed in Chicago Fire) — no substitutes for this period
- Most individual Catholic parish sacramental registers — held at Archdiocesan Archives or individual parishes
- Scott's Blue Book (1939–1965) — microfilm at Chicago Public Library; not digitized or indexed online
- Chicago Urban League records, YMCA records, settlement house records — at respective archives
- Chicago Public Schools enrollment records — at CPS archives
- Cook County Hospital and institutional records

## Known record losses
- **1871 Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871):** Destroyed virtually all pre-1871 records of Cook County — court records, deed records, vital records, and most other civil documents. This is the single largest record loss affecting Cook County research. For events before 1871, researchers must rely on federal census records (1850, 1860, 1870), church records held outside the city, and records that had been copied or transmitted elsewhere.
- No significant record losses are documented for the 1900–1945 period.

## Research tips
- **Search separate African American indexes first.** The [Illinois Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records) FamilySearch Wiki page states that African Americans may be recorded in separate files and indexes — never rely solely on the general series when researching Black families; always search for separate 'colored' registers or indexes.
- **Use the Chicago Defender as a primary source.** For African American families, the Defender (1905–present) is effectively a vital records substitute — it carried birth announcements, marriage notices, obituaries, and 'Migrants' columns listing Southern arrivals by name. Available via ProQuest Historical Newspapers at most public libraries.
- **Cross-reference city directories annually.** Chicago city directories (annual) are available on Ancestry and FamilySearch and place residents at a specific address in non-census years. For a migrant family arriving c. 1916–1930, directories are the most efficient way to establish when they arrived and where they first lived.
- **The 1890 census is gone — plan around it.** Use the 1880 and 1900 censuses on either side, supplemented by city directories, church records, and tax records for the 1885–1895 window.
- **Research African American Great Migration context.** The Ogletree/Pearcy family almost certainly arrived during the Great Migration. The [Illinois Getting Started](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Getting_Started) FamilySearch Wiki page provides general orientation; supplement with Isabel Wilkerson's *The Warmth of Other Suns* for migration context that shapes which records exist.
- **Vivian G. Harsh Collection is the definitive African American resource.** The Harsh Collection at the Chicago Public Library (Woodson Branch, 9525 S. Halsted St.) holds manuscript collections, church records, organization records, and clipping files for Black Chicago that exist nowhere else.
- **Check both county and state vital record series.** For events 1877–1915, search the county birth registers and death registers. For 1916–1945, also search the statewide series (Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths 1916–1948, id 1438856). Both may contain the same event, but with different information.
- **Naturalization searches apply only if the family had immigrant members.** The Ogletree/Pearcy family appears to be African American and native-born; naturalization records are inapplicable unless the tree reveals immigrant relatives.

entry.rationale: Sound basis verification (BCG Standard 11). Locates Lewis Washington Ogletree (~age 18) and Mattie Pearcy in their natal households before the 1905 marriage, confirming their ages, birthplaces, and identities before any child-enumeration conclusions are drawn. Three putative children in the tree (Nellie Mae Ogletree, Harriett Haygood, Lewis Ogletree) have no sourced basis and cannot be treated as established. Two Spalding County 1900 census volumes (imageGroupNumbers 004120084 and 004120083) are 96–97% name-indexed per volume_search. Also search for 'Pearcy' households in Spalding County to locate Mattie in her natal family.

Confirms the 1905 marriage of Lewis + Mattie as the starting-point fact for q_001. The Spalding County 'colored' marriage register volume F (imageGroupNumber 007718973, 1903–1910) is 100% name-indexed on FamilySearch and is the correct register for this African American couple — separate from the general white register per loc_001 quirks. The marriage record establishes the couple as a unit and supplies witness names (likely relatives) that serve as FAN leads for follow-up. Note variant spellings to try: 'Pearcy,' 'Pearsey,' 'Percy,' 'Piercy.'

Dual-purpose item. (1) Fallback for item 2: if Lewis + Mattie's 1905 marriage is absent from colored vol F, search the general Georgia County Marriages 1785–1950 (collection id 1927197, 1.9M records, indexed), which encompasses all Spalding County registers. (2) Primary search for children of Lewis + Mattie who married in Georgia: the Spalding County colored marriage register volume I (imageGroupNumber 007718976, 1923–1933, 100% indexed) covers the decade when children born 1905–1915 would be marrying. A daughter's marriage record names her parents and birth date/place — direct evidence of a child. The putative tree child 'Harriett Haygood' may represent an Ogletree daughter who married into the Haygood family in Georgia.

First post-marriage federal census (5 years into the marriage). Lists every household member by name, age, relationship, and birthplace. The 1910 census uniquely records the number of years married and the number of children born versus children living — direct quantitative evidence toward child enumeration. Lewis (~age 28) and Mattie (~age 25–30, estimated) should appear as head and wife, with any children born 1906–1910 listed. The 1910 U.S. census is fully indexed on FamilySearch. The three putative tree children (Nellie Mae, Harriett, Lewis Jr.) must be confirmed or refuted against this household.

The Great Migration (1916–1940) drew many African American families from Spalding County, Georgia to Chicago. This is searched co-equally with item 6 (Spalding County 1920) because the migration date is unknown. If found in Cook County, it establishes the family had migrated before April 1920 and captures children born 1910–1920. The 1920 census lists every household member with name, age, relationship, birthplace, and parents' birthplace. The 1920 U.S. census is fully indexed on FamilySearch (record_search). Search for 'Ogletree' / 'Ogle Tree' / variant spellings in Cook County.

Co-equal 1920 census search with item 5 (Cook County IL): if Lewis + Mattie had not yet migrated by April 1920, they appear here. If absent from both, that suggests migration occurred between 1920 and the next search point. CRITICAL: The Spalding County 1920 census is browse-only — volume 004300135 is 0% name-indexed and fulltextSearchable: false per volume_search. This item requires browsing by enumeration district via search-images, not a name search. The 1920 census reports the number of children born versus living, a primary quantitative check on child counts.

Lists all household members in 1930, capturing children born 1920–1930 still in the home and older children who may have established separate households (search by their own name). The 1930 census reports birthplace and parents' birthplaces, confirming Georgia origin. By 1930 Lewis would be ~48 and the couple's older children (~ages 18–24) might be living independently — search for 'Ogletree' households throughout Cook County. Fully indexed on FamilySearch.

Last available federal census. Lists all household members, birth states, and 1935 residence (useful for confirming Georgia origin and migration timing). Teenage children born in the late 1920s would still be at home; adult children living separately are findable by name search. The 1940 census is fully indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch. Also search for older children now heading their own Cook County households — surname 'Ogletree' plus estimated birth years from prior census finds.

Cook County Birth Certificates 1871–1953 (collection id 1462519, 3.4M records, indexed) and Cook County Birth Registers 1871–1915 (id 1463129, 962K records, indexed). Children born in Chicago after the family's migration are registered here. Birth certificates name both parents and the child's full name and birthdate — direct evidence of a child's existence. IMPORTANT: loc_002 quirks state African Americans may be in separate files or indexes — search both the general index and any 'colored' series. Date range opens 1906 (one year after marriage) allowing for early migration.

Georgia had no civil birth registration before 1919 (and African American compliance lagged further). Georgia County Delayed Birth Records 1829–1961 (collection id 3438747, 99K records, indexed) contains retrospective birth registrations commonly filed in the 1940s–1960s by adults needing documentation for Social Security or military service. Many African Americans born 1900–1930 in Georgia appear here. A delayed birth certificate names the child's birth date/place and both parents — direct evidence of a child of the couple. Search for 'Ogletree' in Spalding County.

Children who died in either state appear in death records that name parents. Collections: Georgia Deaths 1914–1927 (id 1320969, 305K records, indexed) and 1928–1943 (id 1385727, 553K records, indexed); Illinois Deaths and Stillbirths 1916–1948 (id 1438856, 2.9M records, indexed). Also search for Lewis Washington Ogletree's own death certificate and Mattie's death certificate — informants on parental death certificates are often children, and the certificate names survivors. Death certificates for children provide birth date/place and parents' names.

WWII Draft Registration Cards for sons of Lewis + Mattie. Illinois WWII Draft (collection id 2832983, indexed) and Georgia WWII Draft (collection id 1880573, indexed). Lewis Washington Ogletree (born 1882) falls in the 4th Registration (April 27, 1942, for men born April 28, 1877–February 16, 1897) — his card lists address, birthdate, birthplace, employer, and next of kin (wife or a named child). Sons born 1897–1925 appear in earlier registrations and list their next of kin — often naming a parent or sibling. Draft cards are direct evidence that a son existed. Also search WWI draft registration (1917–1918) for any sons born before 1900.

Cook County Marriages 1871–1969 (collection id 1463145, 1.76M records, indexed). Daughters of Lewis + Mattie adopted their husbands' surnames at marriage, rendering them invisible in records under 'Ogletree.' A daughter's marriage record names her parents and birth date/place — direct evidence of the parent-child relationship. Search for women born ~1906–1930 listing 'Ogletree' as maiden name or listing Lewis/Mattie as parents. The putative tree child 'Harriett Haygood' (surname Haygood) was likely an Ogletree daughter who married a Haygood — search specifically for Harriett Ogletree + Haygood in Cook County marriage records.

FAN cluster search required by BCG Standard 14 for this enumeration/identity question. Searches for all 'Ogletree' households in Spalding County in 1900 and 1910 to identify Lewis's parents and siblings. Lewis's father's household in 1900 establishes Lewis's natal family and confirms Lewis's parentage. Siblings of Lewis who remained in Spalding County may have taken in children of Lewis + Mattie; their households may list nieces or nephews surnamed Ogletree. Establishing the full Ogletree family network also guards against confusing Lewis's children with those of a brother or cousin with similar given names. Both the 1900 and 1910 Spalding County censuses are indexed on FamilySearch.

entry.description: Identity conflict: person-evidence entries pe_077–pe_082 speculatively linked the head of the 1930 Chicago census household (record XSTQ-2BF) to tree person GWXS-RXR (Mattie Pearcy Ogletree, b. Nov 1886, Georgia). Assertion a_133 records the head's name as 'Hattie L Ogletree [?]' and a_135 records her birth year as ~1900 — a 14-year discrepancy from GWXS-RXR's known birth year. The image of the census page (saved as images/ark_61903_3_1_33SQ-GR48-SNM.jpg) confirms the head is 'Hattie H' Ogletree, age 30 (b. ~1900), marital status Single, occupation Stenographer. Mattie Pearcy (b. Nov 1886) would have been approximately 43 years old in 1930 — incompatible with the census image. The person-evidence links to GWXS-RXR must be corrected. Crucially, the census image also shows the four Ogletree-surnamed household members are listed as NIECE and NEPHEW of the head — not as her children — meaning the children's parentage link runs through a sibling of Hattie H, most plausibly Lewis Washington Ogletree.

entry.statement: The head of the 1930 Chicago census household 'Hattie H Ogletree' (b. ~1900, Single, Stenographer, Cook County, IL) is the same individual as the person enumerated as 'Keattie Ogletree' in the 1900 Spalding County, Georgia census for L.D. Ogletree's household (now tree stub I7). 'Keattie' was flagged as a likely misread of 'Hattie' at extraction. If confirmed, Hattie H is Lewis Washington Ogletree's sister, and her custody of four Ogletree children as their aunt in 1930 (relationship column: niece/nephew) is direct census evidence that Lewis Washington is the father of Louise (~1910), Girard (~1911), Willie M (~1913), and Lewis W Jr. (~1916).

**Context:**  
The 1930 Cook County census household (record XSTQ-2BF, src_004) was extracted with the head of household speculatively linked in person-evidence (pe_077–pe_082) to tree person GWXS-RXR (Mattie Pearcy Ogletree, b. Nov 1886, Georgia). This link is WRONG. A census image reader has since confirmed:

This means:
1. The 1930 household head is NOT GWXS-RXR (Mattie Pearcy, b. 1886)
2. "Hattie H Ogletree" (b. ~1900) is a DIFFERENT person — almost certainly Lewis Washington Ogletree's younger sister
3. A conflict entry (c_001) and hypothesis entry (h_001) have been created documenting this

**What to do for Task A:**

Do NOT remove the existing person_evidence links for the children (I9–I12 stubs); instead update/annotate them to reflect that the census relationship establishes them as nieces/nephews of a probable Ogletree sibling.

**3. src_007 (Willa Mae Ogletree + Wilbon McClerkin, 3 Aug 1936 Cook County IL)**

# Locality Guide: Spalding County, Georgia (1900–1940)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 20, 1851 from Fayette, Henry, and Pike Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Griffin, Georgia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Georgia, United States
- **Population during period:** 17,619 (1900) → 19,741 (1910) → 21,908 (1920) → 23,495 (1930) → 28,427 (1940) — per [Spalding County, Georgia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy)
- **Economy:** Cotton agriculture, textile mills (Griffin was a major textile center), railroad junction
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly white and Black Southerners; significant African American population. The Ogletree / Pearcy family is almost certainly African American, given their 1905 Spalding County marriage (recorded in a separate "colored" register) and subsequent Great Migration to Chicago — a pattern characteristic of African American families departing the South between 1910 and 1940.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (predominant among African Americans), Methodist, Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration (c.1916–1940) drew many African American families from Spalding County to Northern cities, especially Chicago; World War I and World War II draft registrations generated records for men in the county

## Boundary changes
- Boundaries were **stable throughout 1900–1940**. Spalding County was formed in 1851 and had no boundary changes affecting the target period. No predecessor searches are needed for events after 1851.
- Neighboring counties: **Butts, Clayton, Coweta, Fayette, Henry, Lamar, Meriwether, Pike** — per [Spalding County, Georgia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy). The Ogletree family may have crossed into these counties; search adjacent county marriage and probate records if Spalding yields nothing.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Births — start date:** Statewide registration began in 1919 at the state level; general compliance by **1928**. No county-level birth registration exists before 1919. Per [Georgia Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records) and [Georgia Research Tips and Strategies](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Research_Tips_and_Strategies).
- **Deaths — start date:** Statewide registration began in 1919; general compliance by **1922**.
- **Marriages — start date:** County marriage records begin at **1852** (county organization), held at county level by the Clerk of the Court of Ordinary.
- **What exists online:**
  - *Births (1870–1960):* Delayed birth certificates — [Georgia County Delayed Birth and Death Records](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3438747) — **indexed + images** — covers children born before registration began who later filed for a delayed certificate
  - *Births (1754–1960):* Church christenings — [Georgia Births and Christenings](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1674802) — **index only**
  - *Marriages (1785–1950):* [Georgia County Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927197) — **indexed + images** — best single collection for Spalding County marriages
  - *Marriages (1808–1967):* [Georgia Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1674807) — **index only**
  - *Deaths (1914–1927):* [Georgia Deaths, 1914–1927](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1320969) — **indexed + images**
  - *Deaths (1928–1943):* [Georgia Deaths, 1928–1943](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1385727) — **indexed + images**
  - *Deaths (1933–1998):* [Georgia Death Index](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1937238) — **index only**
  - *Death certificates (1919–1930):* [Georgia Archives Virtual Vault](https://vault.georgiaarchives.org/digital/collection/gadeaths/search) — **indexed + images** (free)
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration before 1919; no digitized Spalding County birth registers for 1919–1928 (partial compliance years) in name-indexed form — search the Georgia Archives Virtual Vault
- **Pre-registration alternatives for births (before 1919):** Federal census household enumeration (1900, 1910 — children listed by age), church baptism registers, family Bibles, delayed birth certificates filed later

> **⚠️ Critical note for African American research:** Records for African Americans were often recorded in **separate files with separate indexes** throughout this period. The Spalding County marriage volumes on FamilySearch include specific volumes labeled "colored": volume F (1903–1910, 100% name-indexed) and volume I (1923–1933 and 1932–1937, 100% name-indexed). The 1905 Ogletree–Pearcy marriage will appear in **the colored register**, not the general register. Search volume F (imageGroupNumber `007718973`) directly.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist (First Baptist, local Black Baptist congregations), African Methodist Episcopal (AME), Methodist Episcopal
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls
- **Where held:** Local church archives, denominational repositories; some filmed by the GSU — search [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/results?count=20&q.place=United%20States%2C%20Georgia%2C%20Spalding) for Spalding County church records
- **Online:** [Georgia Church Vital Records, 1828–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2790246) — indexed + images (315 records); [Georgia Church Marriages, 1754–1960](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2549568) — indexed + images; [Spalding County Bible Records](http://usgwarchives.net/ga/spalding/bible.html) at USGenWeb
- **Note:** Church records are the primary pre-1919 substitute for civil birth and death registration

### Census records
- **1900 federal census:** Spalding County — **96–97% name-indexed** on FamilySearch (image groups 004120084 and 004120083); also fully indexed on Ancestry. Search by name.
- **1910 federal census:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- **1920 federal census:** Spalding County image group 004300135 — **0% name-indexed (browse-only)** on FamilySearch; indexed on Ancestry
- **1930 federal census:** Spalding County image group 004532000 — **0% name-indexed (browse-only)** on FamilySearch; indexed on Ancestry
- **1940 federal census:** Indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Note:** The 1900 and 1910 censuses are the most important for identifying children born in Georgia before the family's migration to Chicago. The household listing will name each child with their age and birth state.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, annual returns (estate accounts), court minutes, lunacy records
- **Date range:** From 1852 (county organization)
- **Where held / online:**
  - [Georgia Probate Records, 1742–1990](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999178) — **indexed + images** (covers Spalding County)
  - Spalding County probate records 1892–1946 (vol. A-B) — imageGroupNumber `005782189` — **full-text searchable, not name-indexed** (browse or full-text search)
  - Will records 1929–1965 (vol. C-D) — imageGroupNumber `005782181` — **full-text searchable, not name-indexed**
  - Administrators records 1891–1931 — imageGroupNumber `005782491` — **full-text searchable, not name-indexed**
  - Court Minutes 1893–1901 and 1901–1905 — full-text searchable images on FamilySearch
  - [Georgia Wills and Probate Records 1742–1992](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/8635) at Ancestry — indexed + images ($)
  - *Abstracts of Will Book A, 1852–1880* — [FamilySearch Digital Library](https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/idurl/1/705325)
- **Note:** The Spalding County Courthouse burned in 1874 and again in 1981, but **all records survived both fires** (per [Spalding County, Georgia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy#Record_Loss))

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Georgia is a state-land state)
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgage records, deed indexes
- **Date range:** 1852 to present; headright/bounty plats predate county formation
- **Online:** Multiple deed and mortgage volumes on FamilySearch (1852–1911, full-text searchable, 0% name-indexed); [Georgia Deed Indexes, 1927–1979](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/3164) on Ancestry; [Georgia Archives Virtual Vault](https://vault.georgiaarchives.org/digital/) for colonial plats
- **Access:** Clerk Superior Court, Griffin, has divorce, court and land records from 1852

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** World War I (1917–1918), World War II (1941–1945)
- **Record types:** WWI draft registration cards, WWII draft registration cards, WWI Statement of Service Cards, military discharge records
- **Online:**
  - [Georgia World War I Statement of Service Cards, 1920–1929](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3010041) — indexed + images
  - [Georgia World War II Draft Registration Cards, 1940–1945](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1880573) — indexed + images
  - Spalding County military discharge records vol. 1 (1921–1946) — imageGroupNumber `008152618` — **58% name-indexed, full-text searchable**
  - Lewis Washington Ogletree (born 1882) would have registered for the WWI draft (1917–1918) and for the WWII "old man's draft" (1942, for men born 1877–1897)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:**
  - [Find a Grave — Spalding County](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/search?location=Spalding+County%2C+Georgia&locationId=county_508)
  - [BillionGraves — Spalding County](https://billiongraves.com/search/results?cemetery_country=United+States&cemetery_state=Georgia&cemetery_county=Spalding)
  - [USGW Tombstone Transcription Project](http://usgwarchives.net/ga/spalding/cemetery.html)
  - [FamilySearch BillionGraves Index](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2026973)
  - African American cemeteries specifically: [African American Cemeteries in Georgia](http://africanamericancemeteries.com/ga/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records may remain with individual churches or the Griffin Spalding Historical Society (770-229-2432)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Griffin Daily News* (Griffin, GA) — long-running local paper
- **Where held:**
  - [Georgia Historic Newspapers](https://gahistoricnewspapers.galileo.usg.edu/) — Digital Library of Georgia (free)
  - [Chronicling America — Georgia titles](http://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/newspapers/?state=Georgia) (LOC, free)
  - [GenealogyBank Georgia Newspapers](https://www.genealogybank.com/gbnk/newspapers/explore/USA/Georgia/) ($)
  - Ancestry Newspapers.com ($)
- **Content value:** Obituaries (especially post-1920), marriage notices, legal notices

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not applicable as a primary source for this family. The relevant "migration" is internal — the Great Migration from Spalding County to Chicago. No international passenger lists are expected.

### Tax records
- [Georgia Tax Digests, 1787–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/4130006) — **indexed + images** — covers up to 1900 only; not applicable for 1900–1940
- County voter registrations [1844–1942](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3326831) — **indexed + images** — can place a person in the county across years

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1919 birth records (none exist as civil records; only church and Bible records survive)
- City directories for Griffin (early 20th century) — check FamilySearch Catalog and WorldCat
- Individual church membership and baptism registers not microfilmed by the GSU
- Local funeral home records (Griffin has several active funeral homes with long histories)

## Known record losses
**None.** The Spalding County Courthouse burned February 1874 and again January 12, 1981, but **all county records survived both fires** — per [Spalding County, Georgia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy). This is an unusually favorable situation for Georgia research.

## Research tips
1. **Vital registration gap before 1919:** No civil birth or death records exist for events before 1919. For children born to Lewis and Mattie between 1906 and 1919, the 1910 and 1920 censuses are the primary sources. Delayed birth certificates (filed years after the birth) may exist for some children; search [Georgia County Delayed Birth and Death Records](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3438747). Per [Georgia Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records).
2. **Separate African American records:** The FamilySearch Wiki states "Records for African Americans are often recorded in separate files with separate indexes." Per [Georgia Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records). Always search the "colored" registers specifically. The 1905 Ogletree–Pearcy marriage will be in Spalding County marriage volume F (imageGroupNumber `007718973`), the segregated register for 1903–1910.
3. **Marriage records are well-indexed:** All Spalding County marriage volumes 1898–1942 on FamilySearch are 100% name-indexed — a significant advantage.
4. **Great Migration context:** Lewis and Mattie moved to Chicago sometime after 1905 and likely before or around 1920 (the family appears in Chicago-area Illinois records for the later period). Children born in Georgia appear in Georgia censuses; children born in Illinois will appear in Illinois records, not Georgia ones.
5. **Search neighboring counties:** The Ogletrees were in Spalding County by 1905, but relatives may have lived in adjoining Butts, Henry, or Pike Counties. Extended family in those counties may produce records naming Ogletree children. Per [Spalding County, Georgia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Spalding_County,_Georgia_Genealogy).
6. **African American church records:** Baptist church records are a key substitute for missing vital records. The Griffin Spalding Historical Society and Georgia Archives may have microfilmed local church minutes. Search [Georgia Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Church_Records) and the FamilySearch Catalog.
7. **Step-by-step guide:** The FamilySearch Wiki offers [Step-by-Step Georgia Research, 1880–Present](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Step-by-Step_Georgia_Research,_1880-Present) and [Step-by-Step Georgia Research, 1850–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Step-by-Step_Georgia_Research,_1850-1910) — directly applicable to this time window.
8. **Eloping / out-of-county marriages:** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that eloping couples sometimes married in alternate counties (per [Georgia Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Georgia_Vital_Records)). If the 1905 Ogletree–Pearcy marriage does not appear in Spalding County, check neighboring Pike and Henry Counties.
